message.content: Lions (family Felidae, order Carnivora) and zebras (family Equidae, order Perissodactyla) share a very distant common ancestor – the last common ancestor of all placental mammals (Eutheria). In other words, the most recent common ancestor of a lion and a zebra was a mammal that lived roughly 70–80 million years ago, before the split between the carnivore lineage (which gave rise to cats, dogs, bears, etc.) and the perissodactyl lineage (which gave rise to horses, rhinos, tapirs, etc.).
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want the common ancestor of lion and zebra. We need to answer. There's no tool needed. Just provide an answer. Probably they want the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of lions and zebras. Lions are Felidae, family within order Carnivora. Zebras are Equidae, family within order Perissodactyla. So their MRCA would be at the level of mammals, maybe at the level of placental mammals. But we can say that the common ancestor is a mammal from the group Eutheria. Or more specifically, the last common ancestor of the two species is likely a mammalian ancestor that lived around 70 million years ago. But we can give a general answer: The common ancestor of lions and zebras is a mammal that existed before the divergence of the carnivore and perissodactyl lineages, roughly 70-80 million years ago. If we want to be precise: The last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae is the ancestor of the clade that includes all placental mammals, which diverged from marsupials around 160 million years ago. But the specific MRCA of lions and zebras is the ancestor of the clade that includes both the order Carnivora and the order Perissodactyla, which diverged around 70-80 million years ago. So answer accordingly.
